subject: english
chapter_title: Glimpses of India: A Baker from Goa, Coorg and Tea from Assam

concepts.title: A Baker from Goa: The Pader's Place in Village Life
concepts.definition: The Goan village baker, called pader, remains a mixed memory of Portuguese days: his loaves, sweet bread bol and bolinhas for marriages and festivals mark every occasion, and his plump, jackfruit-like figure testifies to good living.
concepts.key_idea: Bakers wore the kabai, a one-piece long dress in Portuguese days, and later shirt and trousers; children ran to him for bread bangles, and monthly accounts were kept in a pencil notebook.

solution_steps.explain: Match occasions to bread: bol for parties, bolinhas for marriage gifts, sandwiches and cakes for Christmas.
The kabai, a single-piece long frock in Portuguese days, later gave way to shirt and trousers below the knee.
The pader's musical bamboo staff announced his arrival; children collected bread bangles, and accounts were tallied monthly in a notebook.

concepts.title: Coorg: Land of Coffee, Rain and Brave Men
concepts.definition: Coorg, halfway between Mysore and the coastal town of Mangalore, is a land of rolling hills with evergreen rainforests, spices and coffee plantations, whose people, the Kodavus, are famed for valour and hospitality.
concepts.key_idea: Coorg's best season begins in September and runs to March, when the air breathes of coffee; its people may descend from Greek or Arab stock, and their dress, the kuppia, resembles the Arab kuffia.

solution_steps.explain: Coorg lies between Mysore and Mangalore in Karnataka, smallest by size but rich in rainforest and coffee estates.
One tradition links Kodavus to Alexander's Greek soldiers; another to Arab origin, reflected in the kuppia resembling the kuffia.
Coorgis have served in the Indian Army, and General Cariappa was the first Commander-in-Chief from Coorg.

concepts.title: Tea from Assam: Legends and the Tea Gardens
concepts.definition: Rajvir, travelling by train with his friend Pranjol towards Assam, sees acres of tea bushes on the hillside and recalls the legends that tea originated in China: Bodhidharma's eyelids and the Chinese emperor's boiling water.
concepts.key_idea: The tea gardens of Assam, with sprouting second-flush leaves from May to July, are a world of green, and Pranjol, born on a plantation, is less curious than his bookish friend.

solution_steps.explain: Pranjol and Rajvir travel to Assam, home of the world's largest tea plantations.
Bodhidharma cut off his eyelids in China, and the emperor's boiled leaves blew into his water, giving tea its origin stories.
Rajvir tells of the second flush from May to July, and the group arrives at Dhekiabari tea estate.

concepts.title: Three Portraits, One Country
concepts.definition: The three parts of the chapter together paint India's variety: a Portuguese-era food tradition in Goa, a martial and natural wonderland in Coorg, and an industrial tea belt in Assam.
concepts.key_idea: Each pen-picture ties a place to a livelihood and a culture, from the pader's bread run to Coorg's coffee and Assam's tea bushes.
question_patterns: compare the three regions described in glimpses of india

solution_steps.explain: Goa shows a colonial memory of bakers, Coorg a hill culture of coffee and courage, Assam a plantation economy.
In each portrait a product or service, bread, coffee, tea, carries the identity of the people.
All three use sensory description, anecdote and first-person memory to bring the region alive.
